vignette:
He is a 55-year-old Middle Eastern man who has spent most of his life working the land. Farming is not just his occupation; it is the rhythm of his days, the measure of seasons, and the way he has always understood himself. He is married, and for years he and his wife have built a life around early mornings, long hours outdoors, and the quiet predictability of tending crops and animals. Before the assault, he describes himself as steady, hardworking, and not easily shaken. He had weathered droughts, poor harvests, and financial stress, but he had always returned to the fields the next day.

The assault happens in a setting that should have felt ordinary and safe. He is alone at the property, managing work he has done countless times before, when he is confronted and attacked. He does not speak about every detail easily, but what stays with him is the shock of it: the suddenness, the sense that his body understands danger before his mind does, and the humiliating helplessness of being overpowered. In the days afterward, he is physically sore, but it is the fear that lingers. He becomes intensely alert to every sound around the house and farm. A vehicle approaching too slowly, footsteps in gravel, a voice raised in the distance, all pull him back into the same immediate feeling that the assault might happen again.

At first he tries to return to work quickly, believing that staying busy will help him feel normal. Instead, the farm becomes one of the places where he feels least settled. He starts scanning the fields before he steps outside, checking locks repeatedly, and keeping tools close in ways that make sense to him as protection. He avoids working alone when possible. If he must go out by himself, he remains tense, listening constantly, and he finds himself turning around to look behind him far more often than he used to. Tasks that once felt automatic now take effort because part of his mind is always occupied with what could be coming from the road, the gate, or behind the barn.

Sleep changes early and profoundly. He falls asleep exhausted, then wakes suddenly in the dark with his heart racing, unsure of where he is for a few seconds. Sometimes he dreams of being trapped or chased, and on waking he feels as if the assault has happened all over again. He lies still so as not to wake his wife, but he cannot settle back into sleep easily. Over time, he grows more irritable and withdrawn. He snaps at small frustrations, then feels ashamed of himself afterward. His wife notices that he speaks less at the table and that he seems far away even when sitting beside her. He does not want to burden her, so he tells her very little, but the distance between them grows in the silence.

He also begins to avoid anything that reminds him of what happened. He changes routes on the property, avoids certain areas where he felt vulnerable, and resists going anywhere that feels crowded or unpredictable. He is uncomfortable when people stand too close behind him. Even ordinary disagreements can trigger a surge of anger or panic if someone's tone becomes sharp. At times he feels as though his body acts before his thoughts do: his muscles tighten, his jaw clenches, and his attention narrows to danger. He is troubled by memories that intrude without warning, especially when something about the weather, a sound at night, or the sight of a stranger brings the event back in vivid fragments.

He does not describe himself as depressed, but there is a heaviness in the way he moves through his days now. Things that used to give him satisfaction, like finishing a row of work or seeing the field come in, no longer reach him in the same way. He still goes out every morning because the farm depends on him, and because stopping would feel like surrender, but he does so with less ease and less trust in the world around him. He remains devoted to his family and his work, yet he experiences each day as if part of him is still braced for the assault to return.
